ann_80.original: Heavy daytime use is the model's main churn signal. Switching this part off lowers training AUC from 0.899 to 0.793. It acts on 1296 of the 4000 training customers; their churn rate is 23.5% against 9.7% for the rest, and through this part it adds 1.76 to their log-odds on average. Threshold: for the typical customer (the model's typical case, with 1 service call) the part is off at 205 day minutes (value 0.00) and on at 210 (value 0.12); from there the whole-model risk climbs steeply, from 3% at 200 minutes to 19% at 250 and 81% at 300. Partner, evening spending: the threshold is lower for customers who also spend more in the evening. At 200 day minutes the part is off with an evening charge of 12 US dollars (value 0.00) but on with 22 US dollars (value 0.62), and the risk moves from 3% to 7%. Partner, service calls: more service calls weaken this part. At 240 day minutes its value is 0.97 with 1 call and 0.09 with 4 calls, so for a heavy daytime user the service-call parts partly replace this term instead of adding to it (whole-model risk 12% with 1 call, 21% with 4).
ann_80.proposed: This part adds to the chance of leaving for heavy daytime users once daytime minutes pass about 210 minutes (between 172 minutes and 242 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way, and more so for customers with a higher evening charge. More calls to customer service weaken it, in an uneven way: for a typical customer it acts on, the chance falls from about 13% at 0 calls to about 3% at 3 calls.

ann_81.original: A second, later hinge on day minutes that adds a little more risk for the heaviest daytime users. For the typical customer it is off at 260 day minutes (value 0.00) and on at 270 (value 0.056), growing with minutes (0.30 at 300). Area code 408 pushes it down slightly: at 320 day minutes its value is 0.30 in area code 408 and 0.46 in area code 415. It acts on 223 training customers, whose churn rate is 59.6%. Its value to the ranking is small: switching it off moves training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8991, so it sets the risk level of the heaviest users rather than their order.
ann_81.proposed: This part adds more to the chance of leaving for the heaviest daytime users, a little less in area code 408.

ann_82.original: Adds churn risk at both ends: for light daytime users and for customers with many service calls. For the typical customer (1 call) it is off at 180 day minutes and grows as minutes fall: value 0.06 at 140, 0.34 at 100 and 0.62 at 60 minutes, which raises the whole-model risk from 3% to 4%. At typical day minutes it switches on at 3 service calls (value 0.11, against 0.00 at 2 calls) and grows with each call (0.61 at 6). Together with the day-minutes ramp this gives a shallow U shape in day minutes: light users get a modestly raised risk, heavy users a steeply raised one. It acts on 1494 training customers, whose churn rate 13.7% is close to the 14.1% overall; switching it off moves training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8954.
ann_82.proposed: This part adds a little to the chance of leaving for light daytime users: more daytime minutes lower it steadily up to about 149 minutes (between 126 minutes and 197 minutes for different customers), then no further. More calls to customer service raise it a little, in an uneven way.

ann_83.original: Adds churn risk once a customer has made 3 or more customer service calls. It acts on 100% of the 848 training customers with 3 or more calls (those with the part off: 0) and on 0 of the 3152 with fewer calls. Threshold: for the typical customer its value is 0.00 at 2 calls, 0.07 at 3 and 0.63 at 4, and the whole-model risk goes from 4% at 2 calls to 23% at 4 and 84% at 6. Evening calls barely matter: at 4 service calls the part's value is 0.641 with 50 evening calls and 0.610 with 150. Of the 318 training customers with 4 or more calls, 50.0% churned. Switching the part off moves training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8838. Service calls also reach the output through their own direct edge (direct_usage_terms), the low-day-minutes part and the service-calls chain, and they weaken the day-minutes ramp.
ann_83.proposed: This part adds to the chance of leaving once a customer has made 3 calls to customer service, in an uneven way; none of the 4000 training customers is affected below that. Evening calls barely change it, and in an uneven way: for a typical customer it acts on, about 6% at 75 calls and about 6% at 125 calls.

ann_84.original: A term that is on for 100% of training customers and changes value for 14 extreme callers, staying at its constant for the other 3986. Below 7 service calls it sits at that constant (value 0.494 at 6 calls in the typical case); from 7 calls it grows (0.517 at 7, 0.988 at 9), adding risk on top of the service-calls hinge. The 14 rows where it varies (its inner unit is on) include 14 with 7 or more calls; it is fitted to those 14 rows. The 14 customers with 7 or more calls churn at 64.3% and already have a mean predicted risk of 93%, so this term changes little: holding it at its training mean leaves training AUC at 0.8989 (against 0.8989). Described, not explained: a small extra slope for a handful of extreme callers.
ann_84.proposed: This part barely changes the predictions: for a typical customer it leaves the chance of leaving at about 3%, in Delaware as elsewhere.

ann_85.original: Adds churn risk for international-plan holders, and much more for holders in Connecticut. It acts on 100% of the 380 training customers with an international plan (holders with it off: 0); among non-holders it acts on the 73 in Connecticut, with a tiny value (0.116 in the typical case), and on 0 non-holders elsewhere. Prediction: for the typical customer an international plan raises the whole-model risk from 3% to 24%; in Connecticut from 3% to 62%. The Connecticut boost rests on the 7 Connecticut plan holders in training: fitted to 7 rows. Plan holders churn at 42.4% against 11.2% for the rest. Switching the part off lowers training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8409.
ann_85.proposed: This part adds to the chance of leaving for customers with an international plan, and much more in Connecticut.

ann_86.original: A large constant applied outside Arkansas, which Arkansas's own direct edge largely undoes. The unit is on for 100% of the 3922 non-Arkansas training customers and for 0 of the 78 Arkansas customers (non-Arkansas rows with it off: 0). Where it is on it subtracts -2.60 from the log-odds (typical case). For Arkansas the gate is off, but the direct state edge adds -2.36 instead of the 0.06 it gives West Virginia, so Arkansas's total state offset is -2.62 against -2.81 for West Virginia. Self-probe: moving the typical customer from West Virginia to Arkansas changes the risk from 3% to 3%; Arkansas customers churn at 17.9% against 14.1% elsewhere. Switching the gate off moves training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8958. Described, not explained: in effect a bias shift plus an Arkansas correction that cancels it.
ann_86.proposed: This part lowers the chance of leaving for customers outside Arkansas; through it alone, a typical customer in Arkansas would be at about 26% against about 3% elsewhere.

ann_87.original: A constant that lowers the log-odds outside Pennsylvania (where it is off) and Michigan (where it is weaker), so it gives those two states slightly higher risk. In the typical case it contributes -0.27 in West Virginia, -0.09 in Michigan and 0.00 in Pennsylvania; the direct state terms give 0.057, 0.057 and 0.057 in those states. Self-probe: the typical customer's risk is 3% in Pennsylvania and 3% in Michigan against 3% in West Virginia. The data only partly agree: the 80 Michigan customers churn at 20.0%, but the 56 Pennsylvania customers churn at 7.1%, below the 14.1% overall, so the Pennsylvania raise looks fitted. Switching the part off moves training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8990.
ann_87.proposed: This part lowers the chance of leaving a little for customers outside Pennsylvania and Michigan, so those two states come out a little higher, though a typical customer is still at about 3% in Pennsylvania and about 3% in Michigan.

ann_88.original: A small risk reduction for New Mexico customers that their direct state edge offsets. The unit is on for the 72 training rows where it acts; the 72 New Mexico customers have it on for 100%, and non-New-Mexico rows with it on number 0. In the typical case it contributes -0.31 to the log-odds while the direct state edge adds 0.39 (against 0.06 for West Virginia), so New Mexico's total state offset is -2.78 against -2.81. Night calls modulate it weakly: for a typical New Mexico customer its value is 5.08 with 40 night calls and 5.83 with 160, and the risk is 3% and 3%. Switching it off moves training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8988. Described, not explained.
ann_88.proposed: This part lowers the chance of leaving a little for customers in New Mexico: for a typical customer, about 2% there against about 3% elsewhere. Night-time calls barely change it.

ann_89.original: A small risk reduction for Mississippi customers that their direct state edge more than offsets. The unit acts on 77 training rows; the 77 Mississippi customers have it on for 100%, and non-Mississippi rows with it on number 0. In the typical case it contributes -0.12 to the log-odds while the direct state edge adds 0.23 (against 0.06 for West Virginia), giving Mississippi a total state offset of -2.76 against -2.81; the typical customer's risk is 3% in Mississippi and 3% in West Virginia. Mississippi customers churn at 16.9%. Switching it off moves training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8990. Described, not explained.
ann_89.proposed: This part lowers the chance of leaving a little for customers in Mississippi: for a typical customer, about 2% there against about 3% elsewhere.

ann_90.original: The linear part of the model for usage, plan and service-call inputs, added straight to the log-odds. The largest direct terms (edge weights per standard deviation of the input) are voice-mail plan -0.71, customer service calls 0.49, voicemail messages 0.18, night charge 0.16, international charge 0.14 and international minutes 0.12. Prediction, voice mail: for the typical customer a voice-mail plan lowers the whole-model risk from 3% to 1%; the messages edge gives part of that back for active users (with the plan, 1% at 30 messages against 1% at none). The 1061 plan holders in training churn at 7.4% against 16.6% for the rest. Prediction, service calls: going from 0 to 2 calls raises the typical customer's risk from 2% to 4% while the hinges are still off at 2 calls (values 0.00 and 0.00), so that rise comes from this direct edge. Holding all these terms at their training means lowers training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8829; the service-call edge alone to 0.8901 and the voice-mail edge alone to 0.8913.
ann_90.proposed: This part adds usage, plan and service-call terms straight into the score: a voice-mail plan lowers the chance of leaving, more calls to customer service raise it steadily, and more international use raises it in an uneven way.

ann_91.original: Per-state linear offsets, one direct edge per state indicator, added straight to the log-odds. The largest weights (per standard deviation of the indicator) are Arkansas -0.33 (offset by the Arkansas gate), Vermont -0.24, Hawaii -0.22 and Washington 0.15. In the typical case the direct state contribution is 1.34 in California and 1.22 in Washington (higher risk), -1.64 in Vermont and -1.62 in Hawaii (lower risk), against 0.06 in West Virginia, a state with no edge of its own. Holding these terms at their training means lowers training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8866. The full per-state picture, with the state gates, is in state_offsets.
ann_91.proposed: This part adds a fixed amount for each state straight into the score: for a typical customer, about 9% in California against about 3% in West Virginia, and below 1% in Vermont.

ann_92.original: The day-minutes and service-call parts add their terms at the output, but they are not independent: service calls weaken the day-minutes ramp, so a heavy daytime user who also calls a lot gets less extra risk than the two effects would give separately. Self-probe on the typical customer (log-odds): -3.66 at 180 day minutes and 1 call, 0.21 with 5 calls, 0.20 at 280 minutes, and 1.60 with both, less than the two separate rises added together; the risks are 3%, 55%, 55% and 83%. In training, 52 customers have the ramp on and 4 or more calls. Switching this whole group off lowers training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.7729, and it holds nearly all of the model's nonlinearity: with every child of the root replaced by a linear fit the AUC is 0.8401, and restoring this group alone brings it back to 0.8988 (full model 0.8989).
ann_92.proposed: This group gathers the daytime-use and service-call parts: heavy daytime use raises the predicted chance of leaving in an uneven way once daytime minutes pass about 210 minutes (between 172 minutes and 242 minutes for different customers), and more so with a higher evening charge. Calls to customer service add to it, in an uneven way, but they also damp the daytime-use rise.

ann_93.original: Each state gets one total offset from the state gates and the direct state edges, which add at the output. In the typical case the total is -4.51 for Vermont and -4.49 for Hawaii, -1.53 for California and -1.65 for Washington, against -2.81 for West Virginia; the typical customer's risk is below 1% in Vermont, 9% in California and 3% in West Virginia. The offsets follow the training churn rates of those states: California 26.8% of 41, Washington 29.2% of 72, Vermont 6.2% of 80, Hawaii 4.1% of 73, against 14.1% overall. Each rests on a few dozen customers, so these offsets are partly fitted to small groups. The group's inputs are the state indicators plus night calls (New Mexico gate); a least-squares affine fit of its output over the training rows has R squared 0.9991: in effect a per-state lookup table. Switching it to baseline moves training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8916.
ann_93.proposed: This group gives each state its own shift: for a typical customer the chance of leaving is about 9% in California and about 8% in Washington, against about 3% in West Virginia, and below 1% in Vermont and Hawaii.

ann_94.original: The model adds the log-odds terms of its children (day minutes and service calls, state offsets, the international-plan gate and the direct usage terms) to the output bias and applies a sigmoid; the decomposition reproduces the network to 4.4e-16. Its main drivers are heavy daytime use, 3 or more service calls and an international plan; a voice-mail plan lowers risk. Self-probe, typical customer with an international plan: risk 24% at 180 day minutes and 1 call, 94% with 5 calls, 94% at 280 minutes and 98% with both; without the plan 3%, 55%, 55% and 83%. Switching off a child lowers training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.7729 (day minutes and service calls), 0.8409 (international plan), 0.8829 (direct usage terms) and 0.8916 (state offsets). Inputs with no connection to the output, such as account length, total day charge and international calls, leave the prediction unchanged: the typical customer's risk is 3% at an account length of 1 and 3% at 240 with 10 international calls, and 3% at a day charge of 50 US dollars.
ann_94.proposed: The model adds up four parts: an international plan raises the predicted chance of leaving for a typical customer from about 3% to about 24%, and a voice-mail plan lowers it to about 1%. Heavy daytime use raises it in an uneven way once daytime minutes pass about 210 minutes (between 172 minutes and 242 minutes for different customers), and calls to customer service add to it from 3 calls upwards. The customer's state moves it from below 1% in Vermont to about 9% in California for a typical customer.

parts.name: churn_model
parts.original_hypothesis: The model adds the log-odds terms of its children (day minutes and service calls, state offsets, the international-plan gate and the direct usage terms) to the output bias and applies a sigmoid; the decomposition reproduces the network to 4.4e-16. Its main drivers are heavy daytime use, 3 or more service calls and an international plan; a voice-mail plan lowers risk. Self-probe, typical customer with an international plan: risk 24% at 180 day minutes and 1 call, 94% with 5 calls, 94% at 280 minutes and 98% with both; without the plan 3%, 55%, 55% and 83%. Switching off a child lowers training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.7729 (day minutes and service calls), 0.8409 (international plan), 0.8829 (direct usage terms) and 0.8916 (state offsets). Inputs with no connection to the output, such as account length, total day charge and international calls, leave the prediction unchanged: the typical customer's risk is 3% at an account length of 1 and 3% at 240 with 10 international calls, and 3% at a day charge of 50 US dollars.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: day_minutes_and_service_calls
parts.original_hypothesis: The day-minutes and service-call parts add their terms at the output, but they are not independent: service calls weaken the day-minutes ramp, so a heavy daytime user who also calls a lot gets less extra risk than the two effects would give separately. Self-probe on the typical customer (log-odds): -3.66 at 180 day minutes and 1 call, 0.21 with 5 calls, 0.20 at 280 minutes, and 1.60 with both, less than the two separate rises added together; the risks are 3%, 55%, 55% and 83%. In training, 52 customers have the ramp on and 4 or more calls. Switching this whole group off lowers training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.7729, and it holds nearly all of the model's nonlinearity: with every child of the root replaced by a linear fit the AUC is 0.8401, and restoring this group alone brings it back to 0.8988 (full model 0.8989).
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: direct_state_terms
parts.original_hypothesis: Per-state linear offsets, one direct edge per state indicator, added straight to the log-odds. The largest weights (per standard deviation of the indicator) are Arkansas -0.33 (offset by the Arkansas gate), Vermont -0.24, Hawaii -0.22 and Washington 0.15. In the typical case the direct state contribution is 1.34 in California and 1.22 in Washington (higher risk), -1.64 in Vermont and -1.62 in Hawaii (lower risk), against 0.06 in West Virginia, a state with no edge of its own. Holding these terms at their training means lowers training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8866. The full per-state picture, with the state gates, is in state_offsets.

parts.name: state_offsets
parts.original_hypothesis: Each state gets one total offset from the state gates and the direct state edges, which add at the output. In the typical case the total is -4.51 for Vermont and -4.49 for Hawaii, -1.53 for California and -1.65 for Washington, against -2.81 for West Virginia; the typical customer's risk is below 1% in Vermont, 9% in California and 3% in West Virginia. The offsets follow the training churn rates of those states: California 26.8% of 41, Washington 29.2% of 72, Vermont 6.2% of 80, Hawaii 4.1% of 73, against 14.1% overall. Each rests on a few dozen customers, so these offsets are partly fitted to small groups. The group's inputs are the state indicators plus night calls (New Mexico gate); a least-squares affine fit of its output over the training rows has R squared 0.9991: in effect a per-state lookup table. Switching it to baseline moves training AUC from 0.8989 to 0.8916.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient); an input the data ties to a category takes its typical value within that category (linked inputs)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

ann_80.text: This part acts on 1296 of 4000 training customers (32%).
For a typical customer it acts on, it clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 2% without this part to about 8% with it.
In the training data, 305 of these 1296 customers had churn.

A higher total daytime minutes clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, and even more so if total evening charge is above 17.12 US dollars (in an uneven way for patients with total evening charge above 17.12 US dollars): for a typical customer, total daytime minutes going from 112 minutes to 249 minutes moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 3% to about 31% if total evening charge is above 17.12 US dollars (with total evening minutes at 234 minutes, as in the data), and from about 3% to about 9% if total evening charge is at or below 17.12 US dollars (with total evening minutes at 167 minutes, as in the data).

Other effects: total daytime minutes past about 210 minutes raises it in an uneven way; a higher total daytime minutes raises it in an uneven way; a higher customer-service calls lowers it in an uneven way.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: a higher total evening charge raises it in an uneven way; customer-service calls depending on total evening charge raises it in an uneven way.

ann_81.text: This part acts on 223 of 4000 training customers (6%).
For a typical customer it acts on, it raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 66% without this part to about 71% with it (on the training data only).
In the training data, 133 of these 223 customers had churn.

Through this part, for a typical customer this part acts on, the model gives a lower predicted chance that a customer leaves if the area code is 408 (about 66%) than if area code is something other than area code 408 (about 71%) (on the training data only).

ann_82.text: This part acts on 1494 of 4000 training customers (37%).
For a typical customer it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 4% without this part to about 5% with it.
In the training data, 204 of these 1494 customers had churn.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: total daytime minutes depending on customer-service calls raises it in an uneven way; total daytime minutes past about 149 minutes lowers it steadily up to about 149 minutes (between 126 and 197 minutes for different customers), then no further; a higher total daytime minutes lowers it steadily up to about 149 minutes (between 126 and 197 minutes for different customers), then no further; a higher customer-service calls raises it in an uneven way.

ann_83.text: This part acts on 848 of 4000 training customers (21%).
For a typical customer it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 6% without this part to about 6% with it.
